overview.title: How convolution works: kernel, reassembly, figure 8.4
overview.main_topic: The second half of the convolution mechanism: each patch is transformed by a tensor product with a shared learned kernel, and the resulting vectors are reassembled spatially into the output feature map; output size can differ from input size because of border effects and strides.
overview.central_idea: One learned kernel, reused for every patch, maps each (3, 3, input_depth) patch to an (output_depth,) vector; placing those vectors back at their spatial positions gives a (height, width, output_depth) output in which every location summarizes the corresponding input location.
overview.importance: Completes the precise definition of a convolution layer (figure 8.4 is the reference picture) and introduces the two reasons output size changes, padding and strides, treated on the following pages.
learning_objectives: Explain the role of the convolution kernel and why it is shared across patches.
Describe how per-patch vectors are reassembled into the output feature map.
State the spatial correspondence between output[i, j, :] and a patch around input location (i, j).
Name the two reasons output height/width can differ from the input: border effects and strides.
prerequisites: Feature maps, filters, and patch extraction (p.260)

summary:
This page finishes the sentence from p.260: each 3D patch is transformed into a 1D vector of shape `(output_depth,)` **via a tensor product with a learned weight matrix, the *convolution kernel***, and **the same kernel is reused across every patch**. The vectors, one per patch, are then **spatially reassembled** into a 3D output map of shape `(height, width, output_depth)`.

Because each vector is put back where its patch came from, every spatial location in the output corresponds to the same location in the input: for example, the lower-right corner of the output carries information about the lower-right corner of the input. With 3 × 3 windows, the book writes that `output[i, j, :]` comes from the patch `input[i-1:i+1, j-1:j+1, :]`, i.e. the 3 × 3 neighbourhood centred on (i, j) (as Python code the slice would need `i+2`; see the note below).

**Figure 8.4** shows the whole process top to bottom: an input feature map with width, height and input depth; several 3 × 3 input patches extracted from it (one highlighted in blue); each patch passes through a *dot product with kernel* to become a column vector of length *output depth* (the *transformed patches*); these columns are assembled into the *output feature map*, a block whose depth is the output depth (the blue column corresponds to the blue patch).

Finally, the output width and height may differ from the input's for two reasons:
- **border effects**, which can be countered by **padding** the input;
- the use of **strides**, defined shortly.

The next pages (p.262 onward) take a deeper look at both.

paragraphs.excerpt: done via a tensor product with a learned weight matrix, called the
paragraphs.what_it_says: Each patch is mapped to an (output_depth,) vector by a tensor product with a learned weight matrix, the convolution kernel, reused across every patch. The vectors are reassembled spatially into a (height, width, output_depth) map. Output locations correspond to input locations: with 3 × 3 windows, output[i, j, :] comes from input[i-1:i+1, j-1:j+1, :]. Figure 8.4 details the process.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A convolution is a small dense transformation (the kernel) applied identically at every location. Two facts follow: the number of parameters does not depend on the image size (only on window size and depths), and the output keeps the spatial layout of the input, so it can be fed to another conv layer. The slice expression is meant as 'rows i-1 through i+1, columns j-1 through j+1', the 3 × 3 window centred on (i, j). In real Python the end index is exclusive, so you would write input[i-1:i+2, j-1:j+2, :]; and in a 'valid' (unpadded) convolution, as in the MNIST model, output index i actually corresponds to input rows i..i+2, which is why the output shrinks to 26 × 26.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Weight sharing explains translation invariance (p.259) and the compact parameter counts in the summary (p.257); spatial correspondence is what makes feature maps interpretable as response maps (p.260).
paragraphs.technical_idea: $\text{output}[i,j,f] = \sum_{u,v,c} \text{input}[i+u, j+v, c]\, K[u,v,c,f] + b_f$, the same $K$ for all $(i,j)$.

concepts.name: Convolution kernel
concepts.definition: The learned weight matrix that transforms each patch into an (output_depth,) vector, reused across every patch.
concepts.intuition: The bank of filter templates, stored together.
concepts.technical: In Keras shape (k_h, k_w, C_in, C_out); flattened, a (k_h k_w C_in) × C_out matrix. Plus a bias of shape (C_out,).
concepts.significance: Weight sharing: parameter count is independent of image size, and patterns are detected anywhere.
concepts.example: First MNIST layer: kernel (3, 3, 1, 64) = 576 weights + 64 biases = 640 parameters.
concepts.misconception: There is not a separate kernel per location; one kernel serves all patches.

concepts.name: Convolution operation (full process)
concepts.definition: Extract patches -> dot product with the shared kernel -> reassemble the vectors spatially into the output feature map.
concepts.intuition: Run the same tiny classifier on every neighbourhood and lay out its answers as an image.
concepts.technical: output[i, j, :] depends only on the patch around input location (i, j).
concepts.significance: The defining computation of Conv2D layers.
concepts.misconception: Deep-learning 'convolution' does not flip the kernel; mathematically it is cross-correlation (beyond the book).

concepts.name: Spatial correspondence
concepts.definition: Each output location summarizes the corresponding location (neighbourhood) of the input.
concepts.intuition: The lower-right corner of the output is about the lower-right corner of the input.
concepts.technical: With 3 × 3 windows, output[i, j, :] comes from the 3 × 3 neighbourhood of (i, j).
concepts.significance: Keeps conv outputs interpretable as maps and lets layers be stacked; it is what Dense layers lose (p.281 notes dense layers get rid of the notion of space).
concepts.example: A response at output[25, 25] in the MNIST first layer comes from the bottom-right pixels of the digit.
concepts.misconception: With valid padding, output index i and input index i are offset by one; the correspondence is by location, not exact index equality.

concepts.name: Padding (preview)
concepts.definition: Adding rows and columns around the input feature map to counter border effects.
concepts.intuition: Give the window room to sit over edge pixels.
concepts.technical: Detailed on p.262; in Keras padding="valid" (none) or "same".
concepts.significance: Controls whether output spatial size shrinks.
concepts.misconception: Padding does not add information; it only changes the output size and border behaviour.

concepts.name: Stride (preview)
concepts.definition: The distance between successive window positions, another reason output size can differ.
concepts.technical: Defined on the following page; default 1.
concepts.significance: A way to downsample within a conv layer.
concepts.example: Stride 2 roughly halves height and width.
concepts.misconception: Stride is not the window size.

math.title: Convolution as shared patch transformation
math.latex: \text{output}[i, j, f] = \sum_{u=0}^{k_h-1}\sum_{v=0}^{k_w-1}\sum_{c=0}^{C_{in}-1} \text{input}[i+u,\, j+v,\, c]\; K[u, v, c, f] \; + \; b_f
math.source_text: Each such 3D patch is then transformed into a 1D vector of shape (output_depth,), which is done via a tensor product with a learned weight matrix, called the convolution kernel—the same kernel is reused across every patch.

variables.meaning: Input feature map of shape (H, W, C_in)
Convolution kernel of shape (k_h, k_w, C_in, C_out)
Bias of filter f (not mentioned on the page; Conv2D includes one by default)

math.operations: For each output location and filter: multiply the patch elementwise by that filter's weights and sum (a dot product), add bias. The same K is used at every (i, j).
math.purpose: Precise version of the 'tensor product with the convolution kernel' described in words and in figure 8.4.
math.interpretation: output[i, j, :] is the vector of match scores between the patch at (i, j) and every filter.
math.intuition: Dot product of the patch with each template.
math.numerical_example: Single channel, one filter $K=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}$, patch $\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}$: output $=3$; patch $\begin{bmatrix}0&0&1\\0&1&0\\1&0&0\end{bmatrix}$: output $=1$. The filter responds most to a matching diagonal. Here indices are for an unpadded ('valid') convolution; the book's centred notation corresponds to window rows $i-1..i+1$.

math.title: Output shape after reassembly
math.latex: (H, W, C_{in}) \;\longrightarrow\; (H', W', C_{out}), \qquad H' = H - k_h + 1,\; W' = W - k_w + 1 \text{ (no padding, stride 1)}
math.source_text: All of these vectors (one per patch) are then spatially reassembled into a 3D output map of shape (height, width, output_depth).
math.operations: Count window positions; depth comes from the kernel.
math.purpose: Explains why output width/height may differ from the input (border effects); strides change it further.
math.interpretation: The output keeps a spatial grid but can be smaller.
math.intuition: One output vector per valid window position.
math.numerical_example: MNIST: 28 → 26 (first conv), 13 → 11 (second), 5 → 3 (third), as in the summary on p.257. The border effect is explained on p.262.

deeper.title: The slicing expression on this page
deeper.body: Note (not in the book): the text writes `output[i, j, :]` comes from `input[i-1:i+1, j-1:j+1, :]`. Interpreted as an inclusive range, this is the 3 × 3 window centred on (i, j). In NumPy, slice ends are exclusive, so the centred window is `input[i-1:i+2, j-1:j+2, :]`. Moreover, for the unpadded convolutions in the MNIST model, output index 0 corresponds to the window centred on input pixel 1, so the exact index relation is `output[i, j] ← input[i:i+3, j:j+3]`. With `padding="same"` (p.262) the centred description holds exactly.

deeper.title: Convolution in a few lines of NumPy
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, a naive implementation of figure 8.4:

```python
import numpy as np
def conv2d(x, K, b):            # x: (H, W, Cin), K: (kh, kw, Cin, Cout)
    kh, kw, cin, cout = K.shape
    H, W, _ = x.shape
    out = np.zeros((H - kh + 1, W - kw + 1, cout))
    Kmat = K.reshape(-1, cout)  # the shared weight matrix
    for i in range(out.shape[0]):
        for j in range(out.shape[1]):
            patch = x[i:i+kh, j:j+kw, :]          # 3D patch
            out[i, j, :] = patch.reshape(-1) @ Kmat + b   # transformed patch
    return out                  # spatially reassembled
```
The single `Kmat` inside the loop is the shared kernel; `out[i, j, :] = ...` is the spatial reassembly.

deeper.title: Weight sharing as a constrained Dense layer
deeper.body: Beyond the book: you could write the first MNIST conv layer as a Dense layer from 784 inputs to 26·26·64 = 43,264 outputs, but with most weights forced to zero (each output only sees 9 pixels) and the remaining weights tied across positions. That Dense layer would have 784 × 43,264 ≈ 34 million free weights; the convolution has 576 (plus 64 biases).

misconceptions.claim: Each output location has its own learned weights.
misconceptions.correction: The same convolution kernel is reused across every patch.

misconceptions.claim: input[i-1:i+1, j-1:j+1, :] in Python gives a 3 × 3 patch.
misconceptions.correction: Python slices exclude the end index, so it gives 2 × 2; the book's notation describes the centred window, i.e. input[i-1:i+2, j-1:j+2, :] in code.

misconceptions.claim: A conv layer's output always has the same height and width as its input.
misconceptions.correction: Border effects (without padding) and strides change the spatial size.

misconceptions.claim: Output depth must equal input depth.
misconceptions.correction: Output depth is the number of filters in the kernel and can be anything.

takeaways: Each patch is turned into an (output_depth,) vector by a tensor product with the learned convolution kernel.
The same kernel is reused across every patch (weight sharing).
The per-patch vectors are reassembled spatially into a (height, width, output_depth) output.
Output locations correspond to input locations: output[i, j, :] comes from the 3 × 3 neighbourhood of (i, j).
Output height/width can differ from the input because of border effects (countered by padding) and strides.

questions.question: What does 'the same kernel is reused across every patch' imply?
options: The number of parameters grows with image size
The layer's parameter count depends only on window size and input/output depth
Each output channel has a different window size
The output has the same depth as the input
questions.answer: The layer's parameter count depends only on window size and input/output depth
questions.explanation: One kernel of shape (k_h, k_w, C_in, C_out) serves all positions, so image size does not matter. Window size is shared by all filters, and output depth is free.

questions.question: In figure 8.4, what happens between the '3 × 3 input patches' and the 'transformed patches'?
questions.answer: A dot product with the (shared) kernel, turning each 3D patch into a column vector of length output depth.
questions.explanation: The figure labels this step 'Dot product with kernel'.

questions.question: The second MNIST conv layer is Conv2D(128, 3) on a (13, 13, 64) input. What is the kernel shape, the number of parameters, and the output shape (no padding, stride 1)?
questions.explanation: Patches have 576 values, each mapped to 128 outputs, plus one bias per filter. 13 − 3 + 1 = 11. Matches the summary on p.257.

questions.question: Why does the lower-right corner of the output contain information about the lower-right corner of the input?
questions.answer: Because each transformed patch is placed back at the spatial location of the patch it came from, and each patch covers only a local neighbourhood.
questions.explanation: Spatial reassembly preserves layout; locality ensures each output location depends only on nearby input locations.

questions.question: Which two reasons does the book give for output width and height differing from the input?
options: Batch size and number of filters
questions.explanation: Border effects (countered by padding) and strides affect the spatial size. Filters/depth affect only the depth; activation and bias don't change shape; batch size is a separate axis.

questions.question: Write the NumPy slice that extracts the 3 × 3 patch centred on (i, j) from input, and explain how it relates to the book's input[i-1:i+1, j-1:j+1, :].
questions.answer: input[i-1:i+2, j-1:j+2, :]. The book's expression denotes rows/columns i-1 through i+1 inclusively; Python's exclusive end index requires +2.
questions.explanation: Off-by-one with exclusive slice ends is a common bug when implementing convolution by hand.

questions.question: Can you redraw figure 8.4 and label each stage with the tensor shapes for the first MNIST conv layer?
questions.answer: Input (28, 28, 1) -> patches (3, 3, 1) -> dot product with kernel (3, 3, 1, 64) -> vectors (64,) -> output (26, 26, 64).
questions.explanation: If your labels match these shapes you have the full mechanism.
